A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same investigation of popularity-related disparities in AI-assisted programming. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, and Appendices A-E are readable and can be matched reliably despite reformatting and additions.

before.justification: v1 reports original code-generation outcomes for 3,011 problems across eight languages and five LLMs, plus framework-development experiments with completion and correction-attempt results.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds C results across the five LLMs. Tables 3-4 and the language and framework figures report empirical outcomes.

M1.justification: The standardized prompts, code-extraction pipeline, API generation procedure, and error-message feedback protocol remain unchanged in Sections 4-5 and Appendix B. Adding C extends evaluation coverage. Appendix D.4 proposes future factorization and clustering work without incorporating it into the method.

E1.justification: v3 adds C to the algorithmic evaluation, expanding coverage from eight to nine languages. The 3,011 problems, difficulty composition, 17 CRUD tasks, and divergent-technology tasks remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Both versions evaluate GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Qwen3-Turbo, together with the same Cursor, CodeBuddy, and Copilot configurations for framework tasks. The framework alternatives are retained. The clustering methods cited in new Appendix D.4 are not evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Table 4 expands the popular-language group from Python, C++, Java, and JavaScript to include C, changing the aggregate comparison against Go, Rust, Erlang, and Racket. The problem set, Pass@1 metric, prompting, decoding parameters, and framework feedback procedure otherwise remain unchanged. This does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The difficulty stratification, error-type analysis, framework comparisons, and application screenshots are retained. C extends the existing evaluation rather than introducing a new diagnostic question. Appendix D.4 discusses a potential latent-factor analysis but reports no implemented analysis, ablation, or robustness test.

E5.justification: Both versions report paired t-tests across 3,011 problems and p < 0.001 for each model in Table 4. No repeated-run information, confidence intervals, seeds, or new statistical estimation procedure is introduced. The changed language grouping and reported mean differences are protocol and result changes.

E6.justification: Table 3 adds five C rows, with Pass@1 ranging from 21.65% for Qwen3-Turbo to 67.78% for DeepSeek-V3; all forty existing model-language rows are unchanged. Figures 2 and 6 add C results. Table 4 revises all five reported mean differences, including DeepSeek-V3 from +49.6% to +44.8%, under the expanded popular-language grouping. Framework outcomes remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs, and the existing metric definition is retained. Appendix D.4 gives a conceptual description of possible matrix factorization and clustering, without introducing a formal objective, derivation, or mathematical result.

C1.justification: The abstract and third contribution substantially qualify the central inference. v1 presents empirical evidence that the Matthew effect emerges and shapes ecosystem trajectories; v3 emphasizes performance asymmetry and an 'AI productivity tax,' explicitly leaving separation of AI-specific amplification from pre-existing structural biases unresolved. This narrows the claimed contribution, although stronger amplification claims remain in the conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive qualifications concerning causal attribution and applicability: AI compatibility need not override runtime performance, adoption decisions are multidimensional, and LeetCode captures only part of software engineering. Section 3.1.2 additionally interprets syntax failures as a warning for broader engineering use. Appendix D.4 proposes disentangling training exposure, documentation, ecosystem maturity, and toolchain fragility instead of treating their contributions as established.

D1.justification: The Reproducibility Statement and Appendix A.2 now provide a repository and GitHub Releases instructions instead of unspecified supplementary materials. The new Ethics Statement specifies LeetCode.cn, restrictions on redistributing problem statements, and an enterprise API access option. Estimated reproduction time changes from 6-9 to 7-10 weeks and cost from $1,500-$2,000 to $1,800-$2,000. Appendix E.2 replaces the explicit MIT-license statement with a repository pointer; core implementation settings remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The introduction adds positioning against the idea of AI as a language equalizer, while Section 2.2 adds productivity and workflow perspectives, citing works including Noy and Zhang, Peng et al., and Weisz et al. Appendix D.4 adds seven references concerning clustering and matrix factorization as possible extensions. The existing code-generation and ecosystem literature remains the foundation.

P1.justification: There are targeted rewrites of the abstract, contributions, related-work discussion, and conclusion, plus new Ethics and Appendix D.4 sections. Author ordering and affiliation presentation change, keywords disappear, and citations switch to author-year style. Most prose and the main section and appendix organization are retained.

P2.justification: v3 reformats the document in an ICLR layout, with a redesigned title block, narrower text area, changed typography, and widespread resizing and relocation of tables and figures. Figures 2 and 6 are redrawn with C bars and explicit model titles; Tables 1 and 3 gain C rows. Existing framework figures and appendix screenshots are retained and rescaled.

improvement.justification: v3 modestly improves empirical coverage by testing C, calibrates the abstract and contribution statement more carefully to the observational evidence, and supplies clearer access and data-handling documentation. These gains remain limited: no analysis resolves causal attribution, stronger amplification claims persist in Section 4.3 and the conclusion, and Table 3 and Figures 2 and 6 still describe eight languages despite including nine. The revision improves breadth and transparency without resolving the central evidential limitation.
